source.title: Scaling Laws Meet Model Architecture: Toward Inference-Efficient LLMs
source.authors: Song Bian; Tao Yu; Shivaram Venkataraman; Youngsuk Park

record.tranche_reason: The study trains architectural variants and evaluates a conditional loss-prediction law, testing architecture effects and cross-size prediction with a method different from the original parameter/token/compute scaling-law measurements.
record.gate_note: The study does not sweep parameter count, training tokens, or compute to test the conventional loss power laws or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation; it explicitly says it does not address optimal allocation of compute between model size and training data. It uses Chinchilla loss as a reference point, then studies architecture-conditioned losses. It also reports many inference-throughput comparisons, which do not measure the claim versions. Individual architecture points in the loss plots are not numerically tabulated, so the curve results are recorded as aggregate figure-only findings.
record.test_reason: At fixed non-embedding parameter count and token budget (100N), the study trains 200+ dense LLaMA-style variants from 80M to 3B that differ in hidden size, MLP-to-attention ratio and GQA, and reports training loss. This directly tests V4, whether shape at fixed N changes loss only slightly, using a different method from Kaplan. It does not sweep N, D or compute to test V1 or V3. Its prediction results concern a conditional architecture-calibration law rather than the parameter/token power law: Lopt below 1B was found empirically, not from a fitted Chinchilla law. Those results therefore bear on no version as stated.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that a conditional extension of Chinchilla laws with hidden size and MLP-to-attention ratio predicts good architectures. The resulting 1B/3B models match or beat LLaMA-3.2 loss and accuracy (+2.1% at 1B) with up to 42% higher throughput. They also find that the U-shaped loss dependence on hidden size and ratio has an interior optimum, and that GQA's effect on loss is non-smooth. They add that outliers harm the fit and that fitting near the target scale is preferable.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits an architecture-aware conditional loss calibration around a Chinchilla reference and predicts architectural choices; it does not reproduce the original parameter/token/compute scaling-law procedure or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Prediction changes with fitting-data scale and inclusion of extreme MLP-to-attention-ratio outliers; joint non-separable calibration performs worse, while additive and multiplicative calibrations are reported as similar.

fits_no_version.finding: A two-step conditional law (an architecture calibration multiplied onto a reference Lopt) predicts the ranking of variant losses at the next size. Spearman is 0.89 (80M→145M), 0.79 (→297M) and 0.75 (→1B), with MSE ~0.0001. The fit from 80M–1B predicts 3B with Spearman 0.50; a fit on 1B alone gives 1.00.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture-conditioned loss offsets fitted at small scale transfer to models several times larger.

fits_no_version.finding: The conditional law's predictive quality depends on fitting choices. Including extreme-ratio outliers drops Spearman from 0.75 to 0.33. Joint non-separable calibration is worse (MSE 0.0067, Spearman 0.21). Additive and multiplicative calibration are equivalent. Coefficients shift with model size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fit-choice sensitivity of architecture-aware scaling laws.

record.problems: The loss-curve values in Figures 4, 5, and 24 are not tabulated. The largest reported conditional-law prediction target is 3B, and the study does not test the conventional loss laws over several orders of magnitude or compute-optimal allocation. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the loss predictions or architecture-loss comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: Individual plotted architecture points in Figures 4, 5, and 24 were not extracted separately because the curves are not numerically tabulated; the aggregate findings and stated curve shapes are recorded in r4-r12. Numerous inference-throughput curves and tables were omitted because they do not measure a claim version. Downstream benchmark values for selected architectures were omitted because the study does not test downstream predictability with scale or pretraining loss.

untested.parts: All: no sweep of N, D or compute to fit a loss power law.
All: no extrapolation of a power law in N/D/C; the prediction tasks concern a conditional architecture calibration.
All: the authors state they do not address compute allocation between N and D.
Depth and aspect ratio (layers are fixed per size); other architecture details; sizes above 3B.
All: downstream scores are reported only for a few selected models.
All as stated: no comparison of N/D exponents or compute-optimal splits across setups.

missing.what: Loss of the exhaustively trained 1B variants across rmlp/attn and d (range about 2.77–2.83), with Panda-1B lowest. This bears directly on V4 at 1B.
Surefire-1B (GQA 9, r 3.6) loss 2.804 vs LLaMA-3.2-1B 2.803, and Surefire-3B (GQA 7) 2.620 vs 2.625. Different shapes give near-identical loss.

record.verdict_notes: The authors frame shape as mattering (U-shapes, interior optimum), but the magnitudes near the optimum and the 1B/3B comparisons are under 1%, consistent with Kaplan's V4. The differences only become several percent at extreme widths or ratios. Figure-axis readings are approximate. V2 and V7 links were removed because the predicted quantity is an architecture offset around an empirically found Lopt, not a power law in N/D/C.

versions.untested_parts: The conventional held-out loss power laws in parameters, tokens, and compute, including their range over several orders of magnitude.

The study predicts architectural-variant losses across a limited size range, up to 1B from fits including models no larger than 297M, and 3B from 1B fits. It does not test prediction across several orders of magnitude or extrapolation of the conventional parameter/token/compute power laws.
The study explicitly does not optimize the allocation between model size and training tokens under a fixed compute budget.
The experiments vary hidden size, MLP-to-attention ratio, and GQA at fixed parameter counts. They do not systematically test depth or every other architecture detail.
Other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, and transfer.
The study reports downstream benchmark scores for selected models, but does not test whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or pretraining loss.

The study tests sensitivity to fitting-data scale, outlier architectures, and calibration form. It does not compare parameter-counting conventions, training schedules, or alternative fitting algorithms.
